newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada posts robust growth in first quarter.
newsitem.headline: Canada posts robust growth in first quarter.

text.p: Canada's economy grew at an annual rate of 3.4 percent in the first quarter, confirming that the country's economic expansion was solidly in place, the government reported on Monday.
Although the number was slightly below forecasts, economists said the headline figure masked the underlying strength of the report.
"By and large, I don't think there's anything here that says that the momentum is braking," said Andrew Spence, senior economist with brokerage Deutsche Morgan Grenfell.

"The GDP figure is a lot stronger than the headline 3.4 percent number suggests," said Sherry Cooper, chief economist at brokerage Nesbitt Burns Inc. "All the domestic components, other than the government sector, were very strong."

With Canadians voting in a general election on Monday, the government statistical agency, Statistics Canada, reported that Canada's first-quarter gross domestic product rose 0.8 percent from the fourth quarter, or 3.4 percent on an annual basis.
A survey of economist had forecast a one percent rise in the first quarter from the fourth quarter.

Statistics Canada said growth in the first quarter was driven by domestic demand. Among the strongest components was a 4.8 percent gain in business investment in plant and equipment and a 1.3 percent rise in consumer spending.

The government agency said the surge in consumer spending was broad-based, with demand strong for all types of consumer goods and service, especially big ticket items. Household borrowing remained high.
"Most of the categories of final domestic demand are very strong for the quarter," said Rick Egelton, deputy chief economist at Bank of Montreal.
Government spending continued to decline in the quarter, with overall government spending falling 0.4 percent, Statistics Canada said.
The agency also reported that the country ran a current account deficit of C$1.22 billion ($878 million) in the first quarter, compared with expectations of a C$1.7 billion ($1.22 billion) deficit.
